missionPremise: That the scraper's private property can be preserved when its trigger moves off Google, by replacing the platform-level OIDC gate with an application-level shared secret the scraper enforces on every request, so the ten Cloud Scheduler jobs — which stay on GCP — can reach the DO droplet. Satisfied as stated: the secret is enforced on every route including the health routes, fail-closed if unset, the ten jobs carry it and no OIDC, and the droplet's port was opened only after the enforcement was proven on loopback. What the premise did not anticipate is that preserving auth is not the same as preserving capacity: on Cloud Run the Chromium lock was per-instance, and on one droplet it is global, so the trigger migration quietly introduced a scheduling-coupling that the old topology absorbed.

warningsForTheNextSession: The droplet's scraper serializes ALL browser work behind one global chromium lock with a 600s wait timeout. That is the single most important new fact about this topology: on Cloud Run the lock was per-instance and contention was absorbed; on one host it is global. Any job that waits more than 600s behind another gets a 500 — observed twice at 19:40Z, when this lane's 750s full-scrape run was holding the lock through the natural 19:30Z fires. The scheduler retry policy (retryCount 2, 300s min backoff, 600s max backoff) recovered wo-manager-sync to 200 36s later; active-wo-report-hourly spent both retries inside the same blocked window. Re-space the schedules, or serialize them deliberately, before treating this migration as done.

A 500 from a Cloud Scheduler job against this scraper is NOT evidence that auth failed. Check the app log line first: every request in this lane's window was `[auth] authorized`, and the 500s came from `Chromium lock timeout` inside the sync. Conflating the two would misread a capacity problem as an auth problem.

`gcloud logging read` on this project returns [] whenever the filter carries a `timestamp>="..."` clause, even for entries that satisfy it. Window client-side. This burned an hour of this lane's verification and made working jobs look unverified.

PowerShell 5.1's ConvertFrom-Json returns a whole JSON array as ONE object, so `@($raw | ConvertFrom-Json)` yields a 1-element array whose properties are arrays and every filter silently matches nothing. Assign to a variable first.

The droplet serves plain HTTP and its port is open to the internet. A shared secret in a header over clear text is replayable by anyone on the path. TLS is owed before this is treated as production-grade.

LESSON: Corroborate every scheduler verification against the target app's own log line (`[auth] authorized POST <route>`). It is one ssh away, it is the direct evidence that the request arrived and was accepted, and it costs nothing — it made an ambiguous log-timestamp puzzle resolvable in one command.
Cloud Logging's AttemptStarted timestamp trails the app's receipt by seconds and the job's own lastAttemptTime agrees with the app, not the log. Two clocks in the same story.
PowerShell -> ssh -> sh one-liners with nested $( ) and nested quotes come back EMPTY, not error. Ship a .sh with scp and run `sh /root/x.sh`.

A .ps1 containing a non-ASCII character (em dash) is read as ANSI by PowerShell 5.1 and the mangled byte sequence breaks the string containing it, even when the file is valid UTF-8 on disk. Keep generated scripts ASCII.

Assigning a provider object (FileInfo-like) into a field and then ConvertTo-Json produced a 4 MB artifact by dumping .NET's entire type table. Use [System.IO.File]::ReadAllText, cast to [string], and assert artifact size before writing.
